# Umbraco Rules

Project conventions, enforced by code in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco` where possible. The short version of the ten UmbraCommandments.

1. **Never put content behind a composition.** Removing a composition permanently deletes its content on every document that used it — no recovery through revisions. Compositions are for meta, settings, CTAs. Litmus test: *if we remove this composition later, is what remains still viable content?*
2. **There are six kinds of document type — file each in its folder.** Page (renders), Block (renders; lives in block list/grid; never used as a composition), Composition (composed onto others; never rendered, never pickable), Data (element; never renders — settings, events, people), Repository (container node; never renders), Repository Item (the pickable records inside a Repository).
3. **Data types never sit at the root of the data type tree.** Built-ins under `/Umbraco/<editor>`, custom ones under `/Custom/<editor>`. `DataTypeSavedHandler` enforces this on every save.
4. **Register in an `IComposer`, not Program.cs.** If `IUmbracoBuilder` can do it, it belongs in `Composers/`. Non-Umbraco concerns (CORS, App Insights) go in `WebApplicationBuilder` extension methods.
5. **Production runs in production mode.** Umbraco Application Url set, `--configuration Release`, HTTPS only, no model generation, no template editing. `appsettings.json` ships configured this way — don't soften it; put dev conveniences in `appsettings.Development.json`.
6. **Aliases are English and camelCase.** No exceptions.
7. **Dictionary keys are PascalCase with dots** (`My.Dictionary.Item`), and a dictionary folder never has values of its own.
8. **Media always lives in a folder.**
9. **The content root only holds Repositories.** The site hangs under the WWW `siteRoot` node; going multi-site means adding another Page beneath it, not re-architecting. Because WWW never renders, the site Page needs a **domain** or nothing answers on `/` — assign `/` for a single site, a hostname each for several.
10. **uSync everything — commit `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/uSync/`.** Export is automatic; you should not need to trigger it. On Umbraco Cloud, use Umbraco Deploy instead.

input.name: Why MCP Is Awesome: Giving AI Real Hands on Your Systems

values.value: MCP turns an AI agent from a text generator into something that can actually look at — and change — your running systems. Here's why that matters.
A protocol, not another chatbot

value.markup: Most people's first encounter with AI is a chat window. MCP is about everything chat windows don't do: giving a model a structured, permissioned way to call real tools — read a database, create a page, upload a file — and get a real result back, not a guess.

values.value: MCP servers are built to fit one specific socket — your systems, described once and reused everywhere.
One protocol, every tool

value.markup: Before MCP, every integration between a model and a piece of software was bespoke: a custom plugin here, a hand-rolled function schema there. MCP standardises the handshake — discovery, authentication, typed calls, structured results — so a server written once works with any MCP-aware client. Build the Umbraco server once; every agent that speaks MCP can manage content through it.

values.value: The best tools don't ask you to describe your problem in English twice — once to a person, once to an API. MCP lets the agent read the same structured contract the humans built the software around.
A happy MCP user
It keeps humans in control

value.markup: Every MCP server defines exactly what it exposes. An Umbraco MCP server can offer document, media and data-type operations without ever handing over a database connection string or a shell. That's a sharper boundary than most 'give the AI admin access' integrations end up with — and it's auditable: every call is a named tool with a schema.

values.value: Each tool call is explicit and typed — easy to log, easy to review, easy to reason about.

input.name: Beyond Chatbots: How MCP Turns Claude into a Teammate Inside Umbraco

values.value: This whole blog — document types, media, content — was built live through MCP tool calls. Here's what that actually looked like, and why it's a preview of how CMS work changes.
Built by MCP calls, not by hand

value.markup: Everything on this site — the block types, the data types, the pages you're reading right now — was created through calls to Umbraco's MCP server: create-element-type, create-data-type, create-document, publish-document. No backoffice clicking, no custom migration scripts. That's the practical meaning of 'MCP is awesome': it's not a demo, it's the actual authoring path.

values.value: Think of MCP as a universal connector: one plug shape, many devices on the other end.
The CMS becomes a tool, not a UI to work around

value.markup: Traditionally, automating content work means screen-scraping a backoffice or writing one-off scripts against an internal API. An MCP server flips that: the CMS's own operations — create a document type, move it into a folder, publish a page — are exposed as typed, discoverable tools. The agent doesn't need a bespoke adapter for Umbraco specifically; it needs to speak MCP, and Umbraco already does.

values.value: We didn't write a line of migration code for this blog. We described the content model, and the server built it.

What this means for teams

value.markup: An editor can ask an agent to draft a landing page from a brief; a developer can ask it to scaffold a document type from a spec. Because the MCP server speaks Umbraco's real structural rules — folders, compositions, block grid shapes — the result isn't a pile of guesswork, it's content and types indistinguishable from what a person would have built by hand.

variants.name: Why MCP Is Awesome: Giving AI Real Hands on Your Systems

values.value: MCP turns an AI agent from a text generator into something that can actually look at — and change — your running systems. Here's why that matters.
A protocol, not another chatbot

value.markup: Most people's first encounter with AI is a chat window. MCP is about everything chat windows don't do: giving a model a structured, permissioned way to call real tools — read a database, create a page, upload a file — and get a real result back, not a guess.

values.value: MCP servers are built to fit one specific socket — your systems, described once and reused everywhere.
One protocol, every tool

value.markup: Before MCP, every integration between a model and a piece of software was bespoke: a custom plugin here, a hand-rolled function schema there. MCP standardises the handshake — discovery, authentication, typed calls, structured results — so a server written once works with any MCP-aware client. Build the Umbraco server once; every agent that speaks MCP can manage content through it.

values.value: The best tools don't ask you to describe your problem in English twice — once to a person, once to an API. MCP lets the agent read the same structured contract the humans built the software around.
A happy MCP user
It keeps humans in control

value.markup: Every MCP server defines exactly what it exposes. An Umbraco MCP server can offer document, media and data-type operations without ever handing over a database connection string or a shell. That's a sharper boundary than most 'give the AI admin access' integrations end up with — and it's auditable: every call is a named tool with a schema.

values.value: Each tool call is explicit and typed — easy to log, easy to review, easy to reason about.

values.value: This whole blog — document types, media, content — was built live through MCP tool calls. Here's what that actually looked like, and why it's a preview of how CMS work changes.
Built by MCP calls, not by hand

value.markup: Everything on this site — the block types, the data types, the pages you're reading right now — was created through calls to Umbraco's MCP server: create-element-type, create-data-type, create-document, publish-document. No backoffice clicking, no custom migration scripts. That's the practical meaning of 'MCP is awesome': it's not a demo, it's the actual authoring path.

values.value: Think of MCP as a universal connector: one plug shape, many devices on the other end.
The CMS becomes a tool, not a UI to work around

value.markup: Traditionally, automating content work means screen-scraping a backoffice or writing one-off scripts against an internal API. An MCP server flips that: the CMS's own operations — create a document type, move it into a folder, publish a page — are exposed as typed, discoverable tools. The agent doesn't need a bespoke adapter for Umbraco specifically; it needs to speak MCP, and Umbraco already does.

values.value: We didn't write a line of migration code for this blog. We described the content model, and the server built it.

value.markup: An editor can ask an agent to draft a landing page from a brief; a developer can ask it to scaffold a document type from a spec. Everything is built, published, and rendering correctly through Umbraco's own block grid pipeline.

## What I built

**Content model** (via MCP, in the required order: model → content → templates):
- 4 block element types in `Blocks/`: `heroBlock`, `textBlock`, `imageBlock`, `quoteBlock`
